syllabus.head: Basic Concepts
syllabus.text: Review of laws of motion (Newton's 1st, 2nd, and 3rd laws), principle of transmissibility of forces, transfer of force to parallel position, resultant of planar/coplanar force systems, parallelogram law of forces, triangle and polygon laws of forces.

syllabus.head: Equilibrium
syllabus.text: Free Body Diagrams (FBD), conditions of equilibrium of a rigid body in two dimensions, moment of a force, Varignon's theorem, moment of inertia.

syllabus.head: Friction
syllabus.text: Law of Coulomb friction, static and dynamic friction, coefficient of friction (μ), angle of friction, angle of repose, ladder friction, and block wedge friction.

syllabus.head: Trusses
syllabus.text: Introduction to trusses, perfect, deficient, and redundant trusses, determination of forces in simple truss members using Method of Joints and Method of Sections.

parts.text: What do you understand by a perfect truss? Differentiate between perfect, deficient, and redundant trusses.
Write the step-by-step procedure to analyze a statically determinate pin-jointed truss system using the Method of Joints.
With the help of a suitable example, explain the Method of Sections for determining forces in specific truss members.
Explain the concept of equilibrium of a rigid body. State the equations and conditions for static equilibrium in two dimensions (ΣF<sub>x</sub> = 0, ΣF<sub>y</sub> = 0, ΣM = 0).

State and explain: (i) Parallelogram Law of Forces, (ii) Triangle Law of Forces, (iii) Polygon Law of Forces. Derive the analytical expression for the magnitude and direction of the resultant of two concurrent forces.
Explain the Principle of Transmissibility of Forces and Free Body Diagrams (FBD).
What is Newton's second law of motion? Explain, using Newton's first law of motion, why a passenger in a car experiences a jerk in the forward direction when the car stops suddenly.
State the laws of Coulomb friction. Define angle of friction, coefficient of static friction, and angle of repose.

A uniform ladder of mass 10 kg rests against a smooth vertical wall at end A and rests on a rough horizontal floor at end B with μ= 0.3. Find the angle of inclination of the ladder with the floor when it is on the verge of slipping (g = 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>).

A uniform ladder of weight 30 N rests against a smooth vertical wall, while the other end rests on a rough horizontal floor (μ= 0.24). Find the angle of inclination of the ladder to the horizontal when it is on the point of slipping (g = 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>).

A uniform ladder 5 m long weighs 180 N and is placed against a wall making an angle of 60° with the floor. The coefficient of friction between the ladder and wall is 0.25 and between floor and ladder is 0.35. The ladder supports a man of 900 N at its top. Calculate: (i) The horizontal force P applied at floor level to prevent slipping, (ii) If P is not applied, the minimum inclination to prevent slipping.

A body weighing 350 N rests on a rough horizontal table. A pull of 120 N applied at an angle of 20° with the horizontal causes the body to slide. Calculate the normal reaction and the coefficient of friction.

A body weighing 300 N rests on a rough horizontal table. A pull of 100 N applied at an angle of 15° with the horizontal causes it to slide. Calculate the normal reaction and the coefficient of friction.
A 10 kg box is placed on a flat horizontal surface (μ<sub>s</sub> = 0.4). Calculate the maximum force that can be applied to the box without causing it to move.

pyqs.title: Truss Analysis by Method of Joints

parts.text: For the given triangular truss PQR (PR = 2 m vertical, PQ = 2 m horizontal) subjected to a horizontal force of 500 N at joint R, determine the forces in all members using the Method of Joints.

For the truss system loaded with vertical loads of 10 kN, 20 kN, 20 kN, 20 kN, 10 kN at 3 m intervals, determine the nature and magnitude of forces in members AB, AC, BD, and DC by the Method of Joints.
Determine the forces in all members of the cantilever truss shown with vertical loads of 100 kN, 60 kN, 120 kN, and horizontal load of 20 kN.
Determine the forces in all members of the symmetric roof truss carrying 100 N and 50 N loads at its upper joints.
Find the magnitude of two forces such that if they act at right angles their resultant is 10 kN, while if they act at an angle of 60° their resultant is 13 kN.
The resultant of two forces P and Q is R. The resultant doubles when Q is doubled or reversed in direction. Show that P : Q : R = √2 : √3 : √2.
Forces of 20 N, 30 N, 40 N, 50 N, and 60 N act from one vertex of a regular hexagon towards the other five vertices taken in order. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant force.
A coplanar system of 4 concurrent forces (120 N at 60°, 200 N at 40°, 100 N, and 50 N) acts on a body. Determine the resultant and angle of the resultant with the axis.
Calculate the moment of a 100 N force acting at an angle of 60° at point B about point A (d<sub>x</sub> = 500 mm, d<sub>y</sub> = 400 mm).

labs.title: Virtual Pin-Jointed Truss Stress & Deformation Bench
points: Physical 3D Assets:
Modular truss framework (Pratt, Howe, Warren configurations) composed of steel tubular members connected at spherical pinned nodes.
Pinned hinge support at one end and horizontal roller bearing support at the opposite end.
Moveable 3D hydraulic load actuators applying vertical and horizontal point forces (0 kN to 200 kN).
Interactive Controls:
Joint geometry coordinates (x, y), bay spans (2 m to 5 m), and truss height sliders.
Point load vector inputs: Angle (0° to 360°) and magnitude at joints A, B, C, D.
Analysis Mode Toggle: Method of Joints (isolates individual spherical nodes) vs. Method of Sections (passes a virtual planar cut through 3 non-concurrent members).
Real-Time Visual Mechanics:
Solves static equilibrium matrices live (ΣF<sub>x</sub> = 0, ΣF<sub>y</sub> = 0).
Color-codes internal axial forces: Tension members glow blue with outward arrows; Compression members glow red with inward arrows; Zero-force members remain grey.
Real-time tabular output listing exact magnitudes and nature (Tension/Compression) matching exam truss formats.

labs.title: Interactive Ladder Friction & Force Equilibrium Simulator
points: Physical 3D Assets:
Heavy rigid timber/aluminum ladder of length L and weight W resting against a vertical wall and horizontal floor.
Positionable 3D human model of weight W<sub>man</sub> climbing the rungs.
Interactive Controls:
Ladder inclination angle slider θ (10° to 89°).
Floor friction coefficient μ<sub>f</sub> (0.05 to 0.6) and wall friction coefficient μ<sub>w</sub> (0.0 to 0.4).
Climber position slider along ladder length (0 to L).
Real-Time Visual Mechanics:
Real-time vector overlay displays normal reactions (R<sub>A</sub>, R<sub>B</sub>) and frictional traction forces (F<sub>A</sub>, F<sub>B</sub>).

Dynamic stability gauge calculates the impending slip margin: As the climber ascends, if the required traction exceeds μR<sub>N</sub>, the ladder undergoes dynamic slip animation, crashing to the ground.

syllabus.head: Engineering Materials
syllabus.text: Classification of engineering materials (ferrous, non-ferrous, polymers, ceramics, composites), carbon steels (low, medium, high carbon), alloy steels, cast iron (gray, white, ductile, malleable), and industrial applications.

syllabus.head: Mechanical Properties
syllabus.text: Strength, elasticity, plasticity, hardness, toughness, ductility, brittleness, malleability, resilience, and fatigue.

syllabus.head: Simple Stress and Strain
syllabus.text: Concept of normal and shear stress, linear and lateral strain, Hooke's law, Poisson's ratio (μ or ν).

syllabus.head: Stress-Strain Relationships
syllabus.text: Stress-strain diagram for ductile (mild steel) and brittle (cast iron, concrete) materials, proportional limit, elastic limit, yield points (upper/lower), ultimate tensile strength (UTS), and breaking point.

syllabus.head: Elastic Constants
syllabus.text: Modulus of Elasticity (E), Modulus of Rigidity (G), Bulk Modulus (K), and their inter-relationships (E = 2G(1+μ), E = 3K(1-2μ), E = 9KG/(3K+G)).

syllabus.head: Axial Deformations & Beams
syllabus.text: Statically determinate stepped bars, elongation under axial loads, composite sections, introduction to bending stress, derivation of flexure formula (M/I = σ/y = E/R), pure torsion equation (T/J = τ/R = Gθ/L), Shear Force Diagram (SFD), and Bending Moment Diagram (BMD).

parts.text: Sketch the complete engineering stress-strain curve for mild steel (ductile material) under tensile loading. Explain all its salient features: Limit of Proportionality, Elastic Limit, Upper and Lower Yield Points, Ultimate Tensile Strength, and Fracture Point.
Compare the stress-strain behavior of ductile materials with that of brittle materials.
Develop and derive the analytical relationship between Young's Modulus (E), Modulus of Rigidity (G), Bulk Modulus (K), and Poisson's ratio (μ).
Define and explain the following mechanical properties: (i) Strength, (ii) Hardness, (iii) Toughness, (iv) Ductility, (v) Malleability, (vi) Resilience, (vii) Plasticity, and (viii) Proof resilience.
Differentiate between carbon steels and alloy steels. Discuss how carbon percentage and alloying elements affect mechanical strength and hardness. Classify cast iron and give industrial applications.
Derive the pure bending equation for beams (M/I = σ/y = E/R) and state all fundamental assumptions.
Derive the torsion equation for a circular shaft (T/J = τ/R = Gθ/L) and write down all underlying assumptions.
Define principal planes, principal stresses, and principal strains.

A member LMNP is subjected to axial point loads: 50 kN at L, load P at M, 500 kN at N, and 200 kN at P. Cross-sectional areas are 600 mm<sup>2</sup> (length 1000 mm), 2400 mm<sup>2</sup> (length 1000 mm), and 1200 mm<sup>2</sup> (length 600 mm). Calculate: (a) Force P necessary for equilibrium, (b) Total elongation of the bar (E = 210 GPa).

A member ABCD is subjected to point loads P<sub>1</sub>, P<sub>2</sub>, P<sub>3</sub>, P<sub>4</sub>. Calculate force P<sub>3</sub> for equilibrium if P<sub>1</sub> = 100 kN, P<sub>2</sub> = 200 kN, P<sub>4</sub> = 150 kN. Determine the net change in length (A<sub>1</sub> = 1600 mm<sup>2</sup>, L<sub>1</sub> = 0.7 m; A<sub>2</sub> = 625 mm<sup>2</sup>, L<sub>2</sub> = 1.0 m; A<sub>3</sub> = 900 mm<sup>2</sup>, L<sub>3</sub> = 1.2 m; E = 220 GPa).

A brass bar of area 1000 mm<sup>2</sup> is subjected to axial forces: 50 kN at A, 80 kN at B, 30 kN at C, 20 kN at D (lengths 500 mm, 1000 mm, 1200 mm). Find the total elongation (E = 1.05 ×10<sup>5</sup> N/mm<sup>2</sup>).
A rod 100 cm long and 2 cm ×2 cm cross-section is subjected to a pull of 1000 kg force. If E = 2.0 ×10<sup>6</sup> kg/cm<sup>2</sup>, determine the elongation of the rod.
Draw the SFD and BMD for a simply supported beam of span 9 m carrying a uniformly distributed load (UDL) of 10 kN/m over a length of 6 m from the left support. Calculate maximum bending moment.
Draw the SFD and BMD for a simply supported beam with point loads (15 kN at 0.5 m, 20 kN at 1.5 m) and UDL of 10 kN/m over 0.5 m.
Draw the SFD and BMD for an overhanging beam carrying a UDL of 60 kN/m and point load of 20 kN. Locate the position of the point of contraflexure.
Draw the SFD and BMD for a cantilever beam carrying a UDL over its entire length.

A rectangular beam (100 mm wide ×160 mm deep) is subjected to a maximum bending moment of 320 kNm. Determine: (i) Maximum bending stress, (ii) Radius of curvature (E = 220 GPa), (iii) Bending stress at 30 mm from the top surface.

Determine the diameter of a solid circular shaft to transmit 300 kW at 250 RPM. Maximum shear stress τ ≤ 30 N/mm<sup>2</sup> and twist θ ≤ 1° in a length of 2 m (G = 1 ×10<sup>5</sup> N/mm<sup>2</sup>).
What is Hooke's law? A spring stretches by 0.2 m when a force of 50 N is applied. Calculate the spring constant k.

Heavy-duty motorized UTM frame with adjustable upper crosshead, hydraulic lower grip, extensometer clip, and digital load cell.
Cylindrical standard tensile test specimens (Mild Steel, High Carbon Steel, Cast Iron, Aluminum).
Interactive Controls:
Material selector: Mild Steel (ductile) vs. Gray Cast Iron (brittle).
Specimen gauge length (50 mm) and diameter (10 mm) inputs.
Hydraulic strain loading rate slider (0.5 mm/min to 10 mm/min).

3D specimen dynamically deforms: Demonstrates uniform elastic elongation → yielding slip bands → plastic deformation → localized necking formation → cup-and-cone ductile tensile rupture.
Live dynamic charting workspace: Synchronously plots engineering stress (σ= P/A<sub>0</sub>) vs. engineering strain (ε= ΔL/L<sub>0</sub>).
Highlights Yield Point, Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS), and fracture energy area (toughness).

labs.title: Beam Flexure & Dynamic SFD/BMD Visualizer
points: Physical 3D Assets:
I-beam or rectangular beam resting on pinned and roller supports with moveable spans (1 m to 10 m).
Load toolbox: Point loads, Uniformly Distributed Loads (UDL), and applied pure moments.
Interactive Controls:
Beam span length and cross-section dimension inputs (b, d).
Load placement sliders (magnitude and position along span).
Section cut plane slider (x = 0 to L).
Real-Time Visual Mechanics:
Evaluates reaction forces at supports (R<sub>A</sub>, R<sub>B</sub>) live.
Dual-trace graphic panels: Dynamically plot Shear Force Diagram (SFD) and Bending Moment Diagram (BMD).
3D beam displays physical bending deflection curve and color-coded internal fiber stresses (top fibers in compression, bottom fibers in tension, neutral axis unstressed).
Highlights point of zero shear and corresponding maximum bending moment, plus points of contraflexure.

syllabus.head: Measurement
syllabus.text: Concept of measurement, generalized measurement system, sources of errors (systematic, random, gross), and error minimization.

Measuring instruments: Temperature measurement (thermocouples, RTD, bimetallic strip, optical pyrometer), pressure measurement (Bourdon tube pressure gauge, U-tube manometers, diaphragm gauge), velocity, force, and torque measurement (dynamometers).

syllabus.head: Fluids
syllabus.text: Fluid definition and properties (density, specific gravity, specific weight, dynamic and kinematic viscosity, compressibility, surface tension, capillarity).
Types of fluids: Ideal, real, Newtonian, and Non-Newtonian fluids (dilatant, pseudo-plastic, Bingham plastic).
Fluid statics: Newton's law of viscosity, Pascal's law and hydraulic lift applications, hydrostatic pressure distribution.

syllabus.head: Fluid Dynamics & Hydraulic Machines
syllabus.text: Continuity equation, Bernoulli's equation derivation along a streamline with assumptions, limitations, and head forms (pressure, kinetic, potential head).
Working principles of hydraulic machines: Turbines (Impulse vs. Reaction turbines: Pelton wheel vs. Francis/Kaplan) and pumps (Centrifugal vs. Reciprocating pumps).

parts.text: Derive Bernoulli's equation for an incompressible, inviscid fluid flow along a streamline from Euler's equation of motion. State all assumptions made during the derivation.

pyqs.title: Newton's Law of Viscosity & Fluid Classification

parts.text: State and explain Newton's law of viscosity. Differentiate between Newtonian and Non-Newtonian fluids with rheological shear stress vs. velocity gradient diagrams.
Explain different types of fluids: Ideal, Real, Newtonian, Non-Newtonian, and Ideal Plastic (Bingham plastic).
Explain various properties of fluids: Density, Specific Gravity, Dynamic Viscosity, Kinematic Viscosity, Surface Tension, and Capillarity.
Explain the working principle and construction of a Bourdon tube pressure gauge with a neat sketch.
Explain the working principle of instruments used for measuring: (i) Temperature (Thermocouple/RTD), (ii) Pressure (U-tube Manometer).
What are the common sources of errors in engineering measurement? Discuss systematic and random errors.
What is the difference between hydraulic turbines and hydraulic pumps? Explain the working principle of Impulse turbines (Pelton wheel) and Reaction turbines (Francis turbine).
Differentiate between centrifugal pumps and reciprocating pumps. Explain how the steady flow energy equation applies to hydraulic turbines and pumps.
State and explain Pascal's law with a neat sketch and describe its engineering application in hydraulic lifts and presses.

A horizontal pipe reduces from a diameter of 300 mm to 150 mm and carries water at a pressure of 180 kPa in the larger section. If the velocity of water in the larger section is 2 m/s, find: (i) The velocity in the smaller section, (ii) The pressure in the smaller section. Use Bernoulli's equation assuming negligible head loss (density of water = 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>).

A manometer measures the pressure of a tank as 250 cm of Hg. For a mercury density of 13.6 ×10<sup>3</sup> kg/m<sup>3</sup> and atmospheric pressure of 101 kPa, calculate the absolute tank pressure in MPa.
A vertical tube contains an oil of specific gravity 0.95 to a depth of 150 cm. Find the gauge pressure at this depth in kN/m<sup>2</sup>.

The small piston of a hydraulic lift has an area of 0.20 m<sup>2</sup>. A car weighing 1.2 ×10<sup>4</sup> N sits on a rack mounted on the large piston of area 0.90 m<sup>2</sup>. How large a force must be applied to the small piston to support the car?

Centrifugal water circulation loop with digital flow control valve.

Water inlet velocity slider v<sub>1</sub> (0.5 m/s to 5.0 m/s).
Throat diameter slider D<sub>2</sub> (50 mm to 250 mm).

Real-time Total Energy Line (TEL) and Hydraulic Grade Line (HGL) visual overlays.

labs.title: 3D Pelton Wheel & Centrifugal Pump Dynamics Rig
points: Physical 3D Assets:
Turbine View: High-head spear nozzle directing water jet onto double-hemispherical Pelton bucket runner mounted on a dynamometer shaft.
Pump View: Transparent volute casing showing backward-curved centrifugal impeller blades drawing fluid axially and discharging tangentially.
Interactive Controls:
Nozzle needle spear position slider (regulating water jet discharge Q).
Impeller rotational speed slider (500 RPM to 3000 RPM).
Brake drum friction load torque slider (0 Nm to 200 Nm).

Dynamometer torque readout calculates mechanical power: P = (2πN T)/60.
Computes hydraulic efficiency (η<sub>h</sub>) and mechanical efficiency (η<sub>m</sub>) live.

syllabus.head: Fundamental Concepts
syllabus.text: Thermodynamic systems (open, closed, isolated), surroundings, boundary, state, path, process, cycle, thermodynamic equilibrium (thermal, mechanical, chemical), quasi-static process, concept of continuum, intensive and extensive properties.

syllabus.head: Zeroth Law & Work/Heat
syllabus.text: Zeroth law of thermodynamics, temperature scales and thermometry, work transfer (displacement work, non-flow and flow work, pdV work evaluation in isothermal, polytropic, isobaric, isochoric, and adiabatic processes), heat transfer, path function vs. point function.

syllabus.head: First Law of Thermodynamics
syllabus.text: First law for a closed system undergoing a cycle and change of state, internal energy as a property, limitations of the first law, Perpetual Motion Machine of the First Kind (PMM-1).

syllabus.head: Steady Flow Energy Equation (SFEE)
syllabus.text: Control volume, conservation of mass and energy, formulation of SFEE, applications to boiler, nozzle, diffuser, turbine, compressor, and pump.

syllabus.head: Second Law of Thermodynamics
syllabus.text: Limitations of 1st law, thermal reservoirs (source and sink), heat engines, refrigerators, and heat pumps, Coefficient of Performance (COP), proof that (COP)<sub>HP</sub> = (COP)<sub>ref</sub> + 1, Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements, equivalence of statements, PMM-2, Carnot cycle, Carnot theorem, Clausius inequality, and entropy increase principle (ΔS<sub>universe</sub> ≥ 0).

parts.text: State the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements of the second law of thermodynamics. Show the equivalence of the two statements (proof that violation of one leads to violation of the other).

pyqs.title: Heat Engine, Heat Pump & Refrigerator COP

parts.text: What is the primary purpose of a heat engine, refrigerator, and heat pump? Define thermal efficiency and Coefficient of Performance (COP).
Prove that the COP of a heat pump is greater than the COP of a refrigerator by unity: (COP)<sub>HP</sub> = (COP)<sub>ref</sub> + 1.
State and derive the Steady Flow Energy Equation (SFEE) for an open system control volume. Simplify the SFEE for: (i) Steam turbine, (ii) Nozzle and diffuser, (iii) Hydraulic pump.
Define a thermodynamic system. Differentiate among open, closed, and isolated systems with practical engineering examples.
Differentiate between intensive and extensive properties, point functions and path functions.
What do you mean by thermodynamic equilibrium (thermal, mechanical, and chemical equilibrium)? Explain quasi-static process and the concept of continuum.
State the First Law of Thermodynamics for a closed system undergoing a change of state and show that energy is a property of the system.
What are the limitations of the first law of thermodynamics? Explain Perpetual Motion Machine of the First Kind (PMM-1) and Second Kind (PMM-2).
Explain why the entropy of the universe is constantly increasing (ΔS<sub>universe</sub> > 0).
Explain reversible and irreversible processes with examples. What factors cause irreversibility?
State the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics. Why is it so called, and how does it establish the basis for temperature measurement?

Derive the expressions for displacement work done in: (i) Reversible isothermal process (W = p<sub>1</sub> V<sub>1</sub> ln(V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub>)), (ii) Reversible adiabatic process (W = (p<sub>1</sub> V<sub>1</sub> - p<sub>2</sub> V<sub>2</sub>)/(γ- 1)).
Describe the Carnot cycle and derive the expression for the thermal efficiency of a Carnot heat engine with P-V and T-s diagrams. State Carnot's theorem.
Calculate the work done in a piston-cylinder arrangement during an expansion process where pressure is given by p = (V<sup>2</sup> + 6V) bar as volume expands from 1 m<sup>3</sup> to 4 m<sup>3</sup>.

A non-flow reversible process occurs where pressure and volume are correlated by p = (V<sup>2</sup> + 6) bar (V in m<sup>3</sup>). Calculate work done when volume changes from 2 m<sup>3</sup> to 4 m<sup>3</sup>.

A fluid expands reversibly behind a piston from p<sub>1</sub> = 600 kPa and V<sub>1</sub> = 0.03 m<sup>3</sup> to V<sub>2</sub> = 0.09 m<sup>3</sup>. Assuming isothermal conditions, calculate the work done during the process.

A reversible heat engine operates between reservoirs at 600°C and 40°C. The engine drives a reversible refrigerator operating between 40°C and -20°C. The heat transfer to the engine is 2000 kJ and the net network output is 360 kJ. Evaluate the heat transfer to the refrigerator and net heat rejected to the reservoir at 40°C.
A Carnot engine has an efficiency of 60%. If the source is at 527°C, find the temperature of the sink in °C.
A heat engine operates between 500 K and 300 K, absorbing 2000 J of heat from the hot reservoir. Calculate the work done and thermal efficiency.
Determine the heat to be supplied to a Carnot heat engine operating between 500°C and 45°C and producing 210 kJ of work.

pyqs.title: First Law Closed System Cycle Analysis

parts.text: Fill in the missing data for each process of a closed system executing a cycle (Q = ΔU + W):
Process A: Q = 18 kJ, U<sub>2</sub> = 35 kJ.
Process B: Q = 10 kJ, U<sub>2</sub> = 4 kJ, ΔU = -15 kJ.
Process C: W = 12 kJ, U<sub>1</sub> = 3 kJ, ΔU = 32 kJ.
Process D: Q = 25 kJ, U<sub>1</sub> = 14 kJ, ΔU = 10 kJ.

labs.title: Coupled Carnot Heat Engine & Refrigerator Rig
points: Physical 3D Assets:
High-temperature thermal reservoir (furnace source at T<sub>H</sub>), low-temperature heat sink (T<sub>L</sub>), and intermediate refrigerated chamber (T<sub>cold</sub>).
Reversible Carnot heat engine driving a common rotating shaft coupled to a vapor-compression refrigerator compressor.
Interactive Controls:
Source temperature slider T<sub>H</sub> (400 K to 1200 K).
Sink temperature slider T<sub>L</sub> (250 K to 350 K).
Engine heat input slider Q<sub>in</sub> (100 kJ to 5000 kJ).
Real-Time Visual Mechanics:

Color-coded thermodynamic energy streams: Displays heat transfer vectors Q<sub>H</sub> flowing from source into engine, net work output W<sub>net</sub> driving the refrigerator shaft, and heat extraction Q<sub>C</sub> pumped out of cold chamber.

Real-time thermal calculations: Displays Carnot efficiency η<sub>carnot</sub> = 1 - T<sub>L</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> and evaluates (COP)<sub>ref</sub> = T<sub>cold</sub>/(T<sub>L</sub> - T<sub>cold</sub>) and (COP)<sub>HP</sub> = (COP)<sub>ref</sub> + 1.
Clausius inequality meter traces ∮δQ/T = 0 for reversible operation, shifting into negative values if user adds irreversibility parameters.

syllabus.head: IC Engine Basics
syllabus.text: Introduction and classification of Internal Combustion (IC) engines, components (cylinder, piston, connecting rod, crankshaft, valves, spark plug, fuel injector).

Engine terminology: Bore, stroke, clearance volume (V<sub>c</sub>), swept volume (V<sub>s</sub>), compression ratio (r), Top Dead Centre (TDC), Bottom Dead Centre (BDC), Mean Effective Pressure (MEP), Indicated Power (IP), Brake Power (BP), and mechanical efficiency.

syllabus.head: Two-Stroke vs. Four-Stroke Engines
syllabus.text: Working principles, cycle events (suction, compression, power, exhaust), scavenging, and comparative analysis.

syllabus.head: SI vs. CI Engines
syllabus.text: Spark Ignition (petrol) vs. Compression Ignition (diesel) engines, carburetor vs. fuel injection system, ignition methods, compression ratios, and fuel-air requirements.

parts.text: Derive the expression for the air-standard thermal efficiency of an Otto cycle (Spark Ignition engine) with all underlying assumptions. Show the cycle clearly on P-V and T-s diagrams.

Derive the expression for the air-standard thermal efficiency of a Diesel cycle (Compression Ignition engine) with neat P-V and T-s diagrams. Define cut-off ratio (r<sub>c</sub>) and compression ratio (r).
Sketch the P-V and T-s diagrams for an air-standard Dual combustion cycle, explaining each process involved. Derive the expression for its thermal efficiency and state one engineering application.

Differentiate between Spark Ignition (SI) and Compression Ignition (CI) engines based on: (i) Working thermodynamic cycle, (ii) Fuel used, (iii) Method of ignition, (iv) Compression ratio, (v) Fuel-air induction/mixture control, (vi) Thermal efficiency, and (vii) Weight/speed.
Differentiate between two-stroke and four-stroke engines with respect to crankshaft rotation per power cycle, port vs. valve mechanism, scavenging, weight, and thermal efficiency.

Define the following IC engine parameters with a neat sketch of the cylinder-piston assembly: (i) Bore, (ii) Stroke, (iii) Top Dead Centre (TDC), (iv) Bottom Dead Centre (BDC), (v) Swept Volume, (vi) Clearance Volume, (vii) Compression Ratio, (viii) Mean Effective Pressure (MEP), and (ix) Indicated Power.

In an air-standard Otto cycle engine, the temperature at the end of the compression stroke is 650 K and the maximum cycle temperature is 2400 K. If the engine delivers 700 kJ of net work, find the thermal efficiency and compression ratio (γ= 1.4).

The minimum pressure and temperature in an Otto cycle are 100 kPa and 27°C. Heat added per cycle is 1500 kJ/kg. Determine pressures and temperatures at all salient points, specific work, and thermal efficiency for a compression ratio of 8:1.

An engine working on the Otto cycle has an initial cylinder volume of 0.45 m<sup>3</sup>, pressure 1 bar, and temperature 30°C. At the end of compression, pressure is 11 bar. 210 kJ of heat is added at constant volume. Determine: (a) Pressures, temperatures, and volumes at all points, (b) Percentage clearance, (c) Mean Effective Pressure (MEP).
An ideal Otto engine operates with a compression ratio of 8 (r = 8, γ= 1.4). Calculate the thermal efficiency.
Calculate the air-standard efficiency of an Otto cycle engine if the clearance volume is 10% of the swept volume (V<sub>c</sub> = 0.1 V<sub>s</sub>, γ= 1.4).

In an ideal Diesel cycle, initial pressure and temperature are 1.03 bar and 27°C. Maximum cycle pressure is 47 bar and heat supplied is 545 kJ/kg. Determine: (i) Compression ratio, (ii) Temperature at end of compression, (iii) Temperature at end of combustion, (iv) Air-standard efficiency (γ= 1.4, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.004 kJ/kg K).
In a Diesel cycle, the compression ratio is 16 and cut-off occurs at 6% of the stroke. Determine the air-standard efficiency (γ= 1.4).

A diesel engine operating on an air-standard cycle uses 1 kg of air with initial pressure 98 kPa and temperature 36°C. Pressure at the end of compression is 35 bar and cut-off is 6% of the stroke. Determine thermal efficiency and Mean Effective Pressure (MEP).

predicted.text: Showing processes on P-V and T-s plots and proving η<sub>otto</sub> = 1 - 1/(r<sup>γ-1</sup>).

labs.title: 4-Stroke IC Engine Kinematic & Combustion Cutaway Model
points: Physical 3D Assets:

High-precision cutaway 3D engine block exposing cylinder liner, reciprocating piston with compression rings, gudgeon pin, articulated connecting rod, counterweighted rotating crankshaft, camshaft with pushrods/rocker arms, poppet intake/exhaust valves, spark plug, and fuel injector.
Interactive Controls:
Engine Configuration Toggle: 4-Stroke Spark Ignition (Petrol) vs. 4-Stroke Compression Ignition (Diesel).
Crankshaft Manual Angle Rotator (θ= 0° to 720°) or Continuous RPM Drive (100 RPM to 4000 RPM).
Compression Ratio slider (r = 6:1 to 22:1).
Real-Time Visual Mechanics:

Animated mechanical valve timing: Demonstrates intake valve opening during downward suction stroke → dual valve sealing during upward compression → ignition flame front propagation → power stroke expansion → exhaust valve opening purging burned gases.

Synchronous Thermodynamic Cycle Display: As the crank turns, a tracking point moves across synchronized P-V and T-s indicator diagrams, showing adiabatic compression, heat addition, isentropic expansion, and heat rejection.
Live power telemetry: Displays Indicated Power, Brake Power, and Brake Thermal Efficiency.

labs.title: Air-Standard Cycle Thermodynamic Comparator (Otto vs. Diesel vs. Dual)
points: Physical 3D Assets:
Dual-screen thermodynamic workstation displaying synchronized 3D volumetric indicator surfaces (P-V-T surface coordinates).
Interactive Controls:
Cycle Selector: Otto Cycle vs. Diesel Cycle vs. Dual Combustion Cycle.
Comparison Criteria Mode:
Cut-off ratio slider (r<sub>c</sub> = 1.0 to 3.0) and heat addition ratio slider.
Real-Time Visual Mechanics:

Superimposes cycle trajectories on identical P-V and T-s axes: Demonstrates visually why η<sub>otto</sub> > η<sub>dual</sub> > η<sub>diesel</sub> for the same compression ratio, and why η<sub>diesel</sub> > η<sub>dual</sub> > η<sub>otto</sub> for the same peak pressure and temperature.
Real-time calculation readout: Evaluates thermal efficiency (η<sub>th</sub>), Mean Effective Pressure (MEP), and net work output per cycle (W<sub>net</sub>) live as sliders move.
